_guide: Seasons: the voyage's main story. Every finished study session plays the next episode of the current season; a season is a premise played over its beats, then a new one starts.
A premise: id (never reused), title, spot (a trait tag: the crew member in the spotlight is picked from people with it, if any), beats, twists, endings.

A beat: variants (a list of texts, or { text, when } for ones that only fit sometimes), travel (true: the ship arrives at a new world first; the first beat always travels), choice (a question for the break: prompt and options of label, flag, reply).
Choices set flags; texts and endings can check them: "when": { "flags.gave": "yes" }. "rerun": "yes" is true when this premise has been played before.
Twists: one per run, picked so repeats differ: id, at (the beat index it joins), variants. Endings: the first whose "when" fits is used, so put the plain one last.

In the text, {Spot} is the spotlight crew member, {Crew} someone else aboard, {world} and {biome} the world, {ship} the ship, {past.world} an earlier world, {past.season} the last season. Pronouns: {spot.they}, {spot.their}, {spot.them}, and {spot:is|are} right after a pronoun.

variants.text: A message reaches {ship}, very faint: the beacon that guides ships past {world} has gone dark. {Spot} is the first to say what everyone is thinking. Somebody should go and look.
Another beacon has gone dark, this one above {world}. {Spot} remembers the last time, back around {past.world}, and is already pulling on {spot.their} boots.

variants: Ships have been getting lost near {world}. The old lighthouse that warns them off the rocks has stopped shining. {Spot} plots the course before anyone asks.
The lighthouse stands alone on a spur of {biome}, tall and pale and completely dark. Up close it flickers, once, then nothing. {Spot} counts the seconds and says it is not random.
From orbit the tower is a tiny white needle. On the ground it is enormous. Its great lamp blinks every few minutes in a pattern {Spot} writes on the back of {spot.their} hand.
The door at the bottom is unlocked. Inside, stairs spiral up into the dark, and the air smells of old oil and something like toast. {Crew} whispers that somebody lives here.
A small garden grows by the door, recently watered. {Spot} and {crew} look at each other. The lighthouse is not empty.

choice.prompt: Go up the tower now, in the dark, or wait for morning?

options.label: Go up now
options.reply: {Spot} takes the lead with a lantern. The stairs creak. Somewhere above, something hums to itself.

options.label: Wait for morning
options.reply: The crew camps by the door. In the night, the lamp above them blinks slowly, like it knows they are there.

variants.text: At the top, in the lamp room, there is a keeper: very old, very surprised, and holding a teapot. "Oh," they say. "Visitors. You came in the dark, how brave."
Morning light pours up the stairwell. At the top, a very old keeper is waiting with a pot of tea and four cups. "I saw your lights last night," they say. "I put the kettle on."

variants: At the top of the tower the crew finds the keeper, small and silver-haired and very pleased to have company.
The keeper explains: the great lamp has a cracked lens, and without it the light can only flicker. They have been fixing it alone for months, a little every day.
Over tea, the keeper shows them the lens: cracked right through. "I have been patching it," they say, "but my hands are not what they were."
{Spot} studies the crack all session. The lens can be fixed, but it needs a light of its own to set the glue, steady for a whole night.
The glue needs a steady light to set. The keeper's spare lamp burned out years ago. {Spot} looks thoughtfully back at {ship}.

choice.prompt: Give the lighthouse a lamp from the ship, or try to make one out of spare parts?

options.label: Give it the ship's lamp
options.reply: The crew carries the lamp from the galley up all those stairs. The galley is darker tonight. Nobody minds.

options.label: Build one from spare parts
options.reply: {Spot} and {crew} spend the night with wire and an old battery. It hums, it smokes a little, and it works.

variants: All night the lamp burns steady over the cracked lens while the crew takes turns keeping watch. The keeper tells stories about every ship they ever guided home.
The glue sets slowly. The keeper falls asleep in a chair, and {Spot} keeps the watch, listening to the sea of {biome} shift in the dark.
At dusk the keeper pulls the great lever. The lamp turns, and a beam of light sweeps out over {world}, as bright as it ever was.
The lighthouse wakes up. Its beam reaches out across the dark, and far away, a ship that was lost blinks its lights in answer.
Later, {Spot} notices the keeper never drinks the tea. The keeper is a very old robot, built to keep the light and keep it company. "I am not good at being alone," it admits. "I was built for two."
Then {Spot} sees it: something huge and slow passing in the dark beyond the tower, glowing faintly. Maybe the light went out for a reason.
On the keeper's desk is a letter, never sent, addressed to a ship that stopped coming years ago. The keeper turns it face down when they see {Spot} looking.
The ship's own galley lamp now sits in the tower, part of the light that guides ships home. Whenever {ship} passes {world}, the beam seems to linger on it a little longer.
The patched-up lamp the crew built still hums inside the tower. The keeper has painted {ship}'s name on it. Every ship that passes {world} is guided, a little, by the crew of {ship}.
The lighthouse shines again over {world}. The keeper waves until the ship is a star among stars.

variants.text: An invitation arrives, written in glitter: the moon colony near {world} is holding its Festival of Small Moons, and {ship} is invited. {Spot} reads it twice and starts training for something.
The Festival of Small Moons is on again near {world}. {Spot} still talks about the last one, and is determined to win something this time.

variants: Lanterns are going up all over the little moons around {world}. It is festival season, and {Spot} has already found the list of contests.
The festival fills three tiny moons, linked by rope bridges of light. There are stalls of strange food, a band that only plays very slowly, and a lot of bunting.
Everyone on the moons is busy: painting banners, testing kites, tasting soup. The crew is given ribbons that say GUEST and immediately put to work.
{Spot} studies the contests: a cooking contest judged by the oldest person on the moons, and a kite race across all three moons at once.
There are two big contests this year. {Spot} cannot decide, so the crew holds a vote. It is a tie. {Crew} says the captain should choose.

choice.prompt: Which contest does the crew enter?

options.label: The cooking contest
options.reply: {Spot} rolls up {spot.their} sleeves. The galley of {ship} is about to become very busy.

options.label: The kite race
options.reply: {Spot} and {crew} start building a kite out of a blanket and two broom handles. It is enormous.

variants.text: The galley smells of everything at once. {Spot} tastes, adjusts, tastes again, and declares the recipe a secret, even from the crew.
The kite is finished at last. It is much too big and slightly lopsided, and it already has a name.

variants: Preparation takes the whole session. Nobody aboard gets much rest, and everybody is happy about it.
Contest day. Everything goes wrong at once: something tips, something tears, and {Spot} stands very still in the middle of it.
Halfway through the contest, disaster: {Spot} makes a mistake nobody else saw. The judges did not notice. {Spot} did.

choice.prompt: {Spot} made a mistake the judges missed. Tell them, or let it go?

options.label: Tell the judges
options.reply: {Spot} walks up to the judges and explains. There is a long pause. Then the oldest judge laughs and shakes {spot.their} hand.

options.label: Let it go
options.reply: {Spot} says nothing. The contest goes on. It sits a little heavy, all evening.

variants: The results are read out under the lanterns. {Ship} does not win. Not quite. But the crowd cheers anyway, because the crowd cheers for everyone.
Results are announced. Somebody else wins, fair and square, and {Spot} is the first to go and congratulate them.
Festival night: the three moons light up at once, and everybody dances on the rope bridges, very carefully. {Crew} dances with somebody from the colony for a whole song.
At midnight the colony sets small paper moons drifting off into space, one for every wish. The crew sends one up together.
The festival winds down. Lanterns come down, bunting is folded away, and the crew is given a bag of leftover festival cake for the road.
In the morning the moons are quiet again. {Spot} keeps {spot.their} GUEST ribbon on, all the way back to the ship.
An old woman at a stall tells {Spot} that this is the last festival: the colony is moving on after this year, to somewhere new.
And then the storm hits: a dust squall from {world} that sends hats and stalls and ribbons flying.
One of the festival organisers recognises {ship}. They were on {past.world} when the crew passed through, and they remember everybody's names.
The judges give {Spot} a ribbon nobody has ever been given before: For Honesty, painted by hand. It goes on the galley wall, right in the middle.
On the way out, {Spot} goes back and tells the judges anyway. They laugh and say they knew. {Spot} sleeps better that night than all week.
The festival is over, but the crew talks about it for weeks.

variants.text: Near {world}, {ship} finds a mail ship drifting with its engines off, its hold full of letters that were never delivered. {Spot} picks one up. It is addressed to someone on a world not far from here.
Another lost mail ship, this one drifting near {world}. After last time, {Spot} does not even ask. {spot.they} {spot:starts|start} sorting.

variants: A little mail ship hangs silent above {world}, its sacks of letters spilling into the corridors. {Spot} says out loud what everybody is thinking: they should deliver some.
The crew spends the session sorting letters into piles by world. Some are years old. One smells of flowers. One has a drawing of a cat on the envelope.
Sorting the post takes all session. {Crew} makes a chart. {Spot} makes tea. The piles of letters cover the whole galley table.

choice.prompt: One letter has come open. Read it, or tape it shut again?

options.label: Read it
options.reply: It is a letter from a grandmother to a grandchild, about nothing much: the weather, the garden, how proud she is. {Spot} reads it twice and tapes it shut very carefully.

options.label: Tape it shut
options.reply: {Spot} tapes it shut without looking. Some things are not theirs to read.

variants: First delivery: a little house on {world}. The person who opens the door reads their letter on the step and has to sit down.
The first letter goes to a farmer on {world}. They read it, laugh out loud, and insist the whole crew stays for dinner.
The second address leads to an empty house on {world}. The neighbours say the person moved away long ago. Nobody knows where.
Second delivery, {world}: the address is a lighthouse, a bakery, then a field. Whoever this letter is for has moved, more than once.
{Spot} does not give up. Asking around, the crew follows the trail from house to house, and finally to a little boat on a lake.
It takes the whole session of asking, but the neighbours remember: the person moved to the coast, and they still write every year to nobody in particular.
The letter reaches them at last. It is from a friend they thought had forgotten them. They read it on the jetty, then ask if the crew has paper and a pen.
At last, the right person. They open the letter and go very quiet. Then they ask {Spot} if {ship} could possibly carry a reply.

choice.prompt: They want to send a reply. Carry it, even though it is the wrong way?

options.label: Carry the reply
options.reply: The reply goes in the safest drawer on the ship. {Spot} checks it is still there twice a day.

options.label: Find a postal drone
options.reply: The crew finds a postal drone heading the right way and tucks the reply inside with a note: please hurry.

variants: The rest of the letters go to the post office on {world}, with a note from the crew explaining where they have been. The postmaster salutes.
The crew hands over the rest of the sacks at the next post office. The postmaster has been waiting years for them, and makes everyone tea.
At the bottom of one sack is a letter addressed to {Spot}, in handwriting {spot.they} {spot:knows|know}. {spot.they} {spot:puts|put} it in {spot.their} pocket, unopened, for later.
And the mail ship is not empty: its pilot is asleep in a hammock in the back, snoring, completely unaware they have been drifting for days.
Something strange: so many of the letters are in the same handwriting, signed with the same name, sent to people all over the sector.
Weeks later, a postcard finds {ship}. It is from the two old friends, together at last, standing on the jetty, waving at the camera.
The postal drone makes it. A thank-you message arrives a few days later, addressed simply to "the kind ship".
The mail ship is towed home. Its pilot sends the crew a box of stamps.

variants.text: {World} hums. Not loudly: it is a low note under everything, felt in the teeth more than heard. {Spot} puts {spot.their} hand flat on the deck and smiles.
Another humming world: {world}. {Spot} remembers the last one and is already setting up microphones before the ship has landed.

variants: The instruments pick it up before anyone else: {world} is singing. One long, slow note, coming from somewhere deep in the {biome}.
{Spot} spends the session listening. The hum is not one note. It is many, very slow, changing over hours, like a song played for something with a very long life.
The crew sets microphones all over the {biome}. The hum is everywhere, but it is loudest in one place: a crack in the ground, like a mouth.

choice.prompt: Record the song to study, or just listen?

options.label: Record it
options.reply: {Spot} records everything. Back on the ship, played fast, the hum becomes something almost like a melody.

options.label: Just listen
options.reply: The crew lies on the ground and listens until they can hear the song changing. Nobody speaks for a long time.

variants: The crack leads down into caves of {biome}. The hum gets louder, and warmer, and the walls glitter where the lights touch them.
Down in the caves the walls vibrate gently. {Spot} touches one and feels the song move through {spot.their} hands.
Deep in the caves, the crew finds them: creatures like soft stones, hundreds of them, humming together. They are the song.
At the bottom of the caves is a great hollow, and in it, slow round creatures, glowing faintly, each humming its own small part.
The creatures stop when the crew comes close. The silence is enormous. {Crew} whispers that they are frightened.
Everything goes quiet. The creatures have noticed the crew. It is the first silence on {world} in who knows how long.

choice.prompt: The singers have gone silent. Sing to them, or back away quietly?

options.label: Sing back
options.reply: {Spot} hums one note, a bit wobbly. A long moment. Then one creature hums it back, and another, and the song starts again with a new note in it.

options.label: Back away
options.reply: The crew backs away slowly. Halfway up the caves, the song starts again behind them.

variants: Back on the surface, the song sounds different. {Spot} plays the recordings, and finds the song has been the same for a thousand years, until today.
The hum has changed. It is still slow and deep, but there is something new in it now, something that sounds a little bit like {ship}.
The crew leaves {world} at dusk. As the ship lifts off, the whole planet seems to hum a little louder, like a wave goodbye.
Leaving orbit, the instruments pick up the song one last time. {Spot} keeps the speaker on until it fades.
Then {Spot} notices: the song rises and falls with the tides of the moons above. The whole planet sings along with them.
{Crew} notices that the creatures hum lower when anyone aboard is sad. They have been listening to the crew, too.
The pattern of the creatures in the hollow matches the stars above exactly. The song is a map.
Months later, a ship passing {world} records the song and sends it on, puzzled: in the middle of a thousand-year-old melody, there is a short, wobbly note that sounds very much like {Spot}.
The song of {world} goes on as it always has. The crew keeps a recording in the galley, and plays it on quiet nights.
{World} keeps singing. Somewhere aboard, {Spot} still hums it without noticing.

variants.text: The charts say the next stretch is empty: no worlds, no stations, just stars for a long way. {Spot} looks out of the window at {world} as it falls behind, and goes quiet.
Another long, empty stretch of space after {world}. This time the crew is ready: blankets, games, and a list of things to talk about.

variants: Past {world} the ship enters the Long Quiet, a stretch with nothing in it for a very long way. The days get very alike.
Day three of nothing. {Spot} has reorganised every cupboard on the ship, some twice. {Crew} suggests a game. {Spot} says maybe later.
The quiet gets into everyone a little. Meals are shorter. {Spot} spends a lot of time at the window.

choice.prompt: {Spot} has been quiet for days. Ask what is wrong, or give {spot.them} space?

options.label: Ask
options.reply: You sit down next to {Spot} at the window. After a while, {spot.they} {spot:talks|talk}: about home, and the people there, and how far away it all feels.

options.label: Give {spot.them} space
options.reply: You leave {Spot} be, but put a cup of tea down next to {spot.them} every evening. The cups are always empty in the morning.

variants: The crew starts a project to fill the quiet: a giant jigsaw puzzle of a planet none of them has seen, spread over the whole galley floor.
{Crew} decides the quiet needs a radio show. Every evening at dinner, somebody presents it. The shows are terrible. Everybody listens.
{Spot} joins in at last: first the puzzle edges, then the corners, then the hard bit in the middle that is all sky.
One evening it is {Spot} presenting the radio show, telling stories about home. Everyone stays up late listening.
A message arrives from far away, slow and crackly: friends and family back home, all talking over each other, sending love to everyone aboard {ship}.
The relay at the edge of the Quiet catches a message for {Spot}: a recording from home, with a dog barking in the background.
The stars thicken ahead. A world is coming up on the charts at last. {Spot} is the first at the window, and does not look sad at all.
The Long Quiet ends the way it began: suddenly. There is a world ahead. {Spot} says, a little surprised, that {spot.they} will miss the quiet, a bit.
Halfway through the Quiet, a single star nobody can find on the charts appears off the bow. {Spot} names it after someone at home.
And in the hold, behind the crates, the crew finds a small fluffy animal from {past.world}, very pleased with itself. It becomes the ship's cat, sort of.
With the message comes a second voice, very faint, from another ship somewhere in the Quiet: "We hear you too. Good to know we are not alone out here."
{Spot} says later that talking about it made home feel closer, not further. On the galley wall there is a new photo now: {spot.their} family, waving.
On the last night of the Quiet, {Spot} brings everyone a cup of tea, for once. "Thank you," {spot.they} {spot:says|say}. Nobody asks what for.
The ship comes out of the Long Quiet a little closer than it went in.
